idiom_name: Twirl templates (.scala.html) compiled to Scala functions
implementation_notes: Scala's own template facility is Twirl: a .scala.html file is compiled into a Scala function whose body is type-checked Scala, so logic and markup live in one compilation unit, and Play ships it as the default engine while sbt-twirl, maven-twirl and gradle-twirl make it usable stand-alone. Scala 2 additionally had XML literals - expressions embedded directly in markup - which were removed in Scala 3, and JVM engines such as FreeMarker remain available for templates owned outside the build. The classic structure is justified when templates must be edited without a build; otherwise Twirl or a typed builder keeps the page under scalac's supervision.
pitfalls: A template that calls a slow service compiles just as happily as one that only formats: fetch and authorize before render and pass the result in, or the page takes the request thread down with it.
Twirl injects implicit request, messages and flash parameters into every template; keeping the parameter list explicit is what keeps a template testable as an ordinary function.
Scala 2 XML literals escaped or not depending on the sink (Node versus String) and are gone in Scala 3, so template styles built on them break on upgrade.
Rendering to a String before writing the response buffers the entire page in memory; stream through a writer or ByteString for large pages and error handling.
